newsitem.title: JAPAN: Foreigners key to Japan stock market in 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners key to Japan stock market in 1997/98.

text.p: Foreign investors hold the key to whether the Tokyo stock market rises out of the rut it is in or sinks further in the 1997/98 business year starting in April, brokers said on Tuesday.

Dissolution of cross-shareholdings and selling after dividend pay-offs are expected in April, and government pensions are not expected to allocate funds until the "Golden Week" holiday in early May, a "Big Four" analyst said.
"Buying by foreign investors or the absence of it holds the key for the market at the start of the new year," he said.

In the past few months, foreign investors have been stepping up purchases of Japanese stocks, soaking up much of the shares Japanese institutional investors are selling in order to make up for shortfalls in their account books before the fiscal year-end.

"The market expects stocks to decline after April, but if foreigners keep buying, it could develop into the second wave of foreign investor buying in the recovery phase of the stock market that started in July of last year," a general manager at Daiwa Securities Co Ltd said.

Market sources said that in the first two weeks of March, net buying by non-domestic investors in the Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya bourses totalled 348.0 billion yen while Japanese institutional investors were net sellers at 201.1 billion yen.
Also in February, foreign investors were net buyers at 377.8 billion yen while domestic institutional investors were sellers at 229.3 billion yen, they said.
Jason James, a strategist at HSBC James Capel, said that the net buying stance of foreign investors was expected to continue in the coming months.
"Stocks are relatively cheaper compared to bonds and foreign investors are likely to continue choosing them over bonds," he said.
Yukiharu Abe, a technical analyst at ING Barings, said foreign investors are likely to turn their attention to the Japanese market once Wall Street takes a breather.
Although there are still some worries that Japan's economy may slow down, foreign investors appreciate forecasts showing that Japanese firms' earnings are set to grow, brokers said.

"Foreign investors are cashing in on the high technology issues which rallied recently," a broker at a second-tier brokerage said. "They are starting to buy low-priced construction, steel and chemical shares."
Other brokers said foreign investors were also starting to place buy orders for issues which have been under heavy fire lately.
